restoration_note: This teaching describes mystical seeing — the brief opening of the inner eye when the soul is loosed from the body during a short sickness — and the differing manners (uniformly vs. delayed; at the head vs. at the foot) by which the Lord accommodates this loosening to each soul. The surviving Coptic is so heavily abraded ('abgerieben') and lacunose, with two near-duplicate damaged passages (5473–5477 ≈ 5478–5482) and long open lines, that confident restoration is impossible for the great majority of gaps. I have restored only where local context strongly constrains the fill: the verb 'fall forth' in {1} (matched by the apparatus's note 'verb of falling/loosing' and the parallel ϣⲁϩϩⲉⲓⲉ ⲁⲃⲁⲗ in 5462), 'their body' in {3} (the natural housing from which the soul is loosed, the precise locus of the teaching), 'sickness' in {4} (echoing 5459 and the title), 'the hour' in {21} (where the names of the inner things are released — same temporal frame as ⲟⲩⲛⲟⲩ ⲛⲟⲩⲱⲧ in 5465), and 'the hour' in {64} (the hour that has reached this man, matched by the surviving ⲡⲛⲉⲩ in the same sentence). All other gaps — the long abraded stretches, the rubbed-off line edges, and the destroyed passages — are marked unrestorable rather than smoothed over with invention.

coptic_restorations.basis: Eight characters rubbed off at start of line; could be a participial or circumstantial introducing 'a brief sickness,' but no traces constrain the syntax. Honest non-restoration.

The apparatus notes 'possibly verb of falling/loosing'; ϩ is preserved at the line edge as the start of ϩⲉⲓⲉ. The parallel construction ϣⲁϩϩⲉⲓⲉ ⲁⲃⲁⲗ ('habitually falls forth') appears in the very next section (5462), so 'who habitually fall forth' is the natural reading for these men whose souls are loosed during the brief affliction.
Only two characters; could be ⲍⲏ (heart), ⲣⲟ (mouth), ⲛⲟⲩ (hour) prefixed to ⲧⲟⲩ. The clause 'their X, whose soul is loosed' does not uniquely fix the body-part term. Unrestorable.

ϩⲙ̄ (in/from) is preserved before the gap; the clause says 'whose soul is loosed forth from {3}.' The teaching is precisely about the soul being briefly loosed from the body during sickness so the inner eye sees. ⲡⲟⲩⲥⲱⲙⲁ ('their body') fits the spiritual register and the ~10-character span.

ⲛ̄ⲟⲩ- ('in a') opens the gap and ⲉϣⲁϩϩⲉⲓⲉ ⲁⲃⲁⲗ ('which habitually falls forth') closes it. The opening section (5459) names ϣⲱⲛⲉ ⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲕⲟⲩⲓ̈ as the sickness that triggers the loosening; this segment continues that thought: 'in a sickness which habitually falls upon (the man).' Five characters fits within the six-character span.
ϩⲓⲭⲙ̄ ('upon') is preserved before a 10-character gap. Possibilities include ⲡⲣⲱⲙⲉ, ⲡⲟⲩⲥⲱⲙⲁ, ⲡⲓⲣⲱⲙⲉ ⲛⲓⲙ — none uniquely constrained. Unrestorable.
ⲧⲧⲙⲁϩ- is the ordinal prefix; the ordinal could be 'second,' 'third,' or higher, and what follows could be a noun governed by it. No constraint.

The Reading explicitly names this as 'the hour' at which the inner names are loosed. ⲡⲛⲉⲩ ('the hour') fits the three-character span and the temporal register established by ⲟⲩⲛⲟⲩ ⲛⲟⲩⲱⲧ in 5465 and ⲡⲛⲉⲩ ⲉⲧⲟⲩ- in 5490.
